title: What Bukangi the shark in South Korea tells us about climate change
description:
For weeks, the city of Busan in South Korea has been playing host to an unexpected visitor. A Dusky shark nicknamed Bukangi. She swam into a canal in the city and simply won’t leave, despite efforts from experts to try to coax her back to the to the open sea.

Those attempts to move her have been live-streamed and Bukangi has become something of a celeb in Busan. There’s merchandise of her, posters with her as a cartoon have been put up and she’s been made the city’s un-official mascot.

Bukangi has helped boost visitors to the city - but what does she tell us about climate change? We hear from the BBC’s Jake Kwon, who’s in Busan, about the impact she’s had on the city, shark enthusiast @SarahShark tells us all about Dusky sharks and our climate reporter Esme Stallard explains why she might be there in the first place.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討南韓釜山運河意外出現灰真鯊 Bukangi 的現象與氣候變遷警訊。這條長約 3 公尺的雌性灰真鯊自 9 月中旬進入狹窄運河後便滯留不去，吸引超過 160 萬名民眾圍觀，並成為釜山市的熱門吉祥物。專家與 BBC 記者指出，灰真鯊 Bukangi 可能因海洋變暖與追逐魚群而迷航，目前已出現壓力與健康下降的跡象。雖然救援人員嘗試引導她重返外海，但此事件也凸顯了氣候變遷、過度捕撈及海洋噪音對全球海洋生態的嚴重威脅。
summaryEn: This episode examines why Bukangi, a three-meter female Dusky shark, swam into a canal in Busan, South Korea, and refused to leave. Arriving in mid-September, she quickly became a local celebrity and unofficial city mascot, attracting over 1.6 million visitors. As experts attempt to guide her back to the open ocean, her situation is becoming urgent as she shows signs of stress and declining health. BBC reporters and experts discuss how rising ocean temperatures, changing prey movements, overfishing, and human activity are driving marine life into unexpected environments, serving as a warning sign of climate change's impact on ocean ecosystems.
